answer.answer:
Concrete construction becomes circular mainly by designing the joints so components can come apart again and by carrying traceable component data through the life of the building: reversible connections instead of glued and monolithic ones are what makes material recovery possible at all, and component data or material passports are what make that recovery economically viable rather than merely technically possible. The payoff recorded is material and energy saving and reduced CO2 and waste, and the same traceable data also takes the cost and investment uncertainty out of deciding whether disassembled elements are worth recovering. Two cautions: circular construction is a thin part of this record, active in only 8 of the 50 coded cases, and nothing concrete-specific and no deployed project sits behind the circularity route here, so treat the material below as the general design logic rather than as a proven concrete practice. Material testing is the strongest thing found alongside circular design in the coded cases, which for concrete is where the practical work would sit.

**The dependency route into and out of circular design**

Circular construction/DfDisAssembly (VA15) carries exactly one inbound and one outbound dependency edge, and both are in front of me, so this pair is the whole directional picture for it in the graph.

Inbound: traceable/linked data (VA9) enables circular construction (VA15), because component data and material passports make recovery and reuse economically viable [1], on peer-reviewed evidence (DEP69). Traceable data is the better-established of the two, active in 26 of the 50 coded cases against 8 for circular design itself, so the data layer is in place in far more projects than the circular intent it could support.

Outbound: circular construction (VA15) enables material and energy saving and reduced CO2 and waste (VA4), on the finding that glued and monolithic joints limit salvage potential while reversible connection design enables material recovery [2], again peer-reviewed (DEP52). That is the single clearest lever for concrete: monolithic casting and glued or grouted joints are precisely the detailing that forecloses recovery, so the decision is made at the connection detail, not at demolition. VA4 is activated in 15 of the 50 coded cases.

A third edge is worth adding because it attacks the commercial objection: traceable data (VA9) mitigates increased cost and investment uncertainty (RI3), since material passports reduce uncertainty about the circular potential and economics of disassembled elements [3] (DEP70, peer-reviewed). Increased cost and investment uncertainty (RI3) is itself among the enablers most often coded alongside circular construction, at weight 6, so the risk and its mitigation both sit in the same territory.

**What sits alongside it in the coded cases (correlation, not dependency)**

The co-occurrence list for VA15 is a cut of 125 co-occurring enablers, not a complete list, so nothing here licenses a closed claim. Within that cut, material testing (PR10) is the strongest association at weight 8, then integrate supply chain (VA14) at 7, then modularisation (PR5), early contractor involvement (CO11), DfMA for DFAB process (PR9) and excavation/transportation (PR16) at 6 each, with design engineer (AC3) and bespoke/customised design (AT1) at 5, CNC machines (RE7) and subtractive manufacturing (PR7) at 4 [4]. These are statistical companions: no direction of influence is asserted for any of them. The pattern is nonetheless legible as a design-and-supply route, with modularisation (PR5, active in 10 of 50 cases) and early contractor involvement (CO11, 14 of 50) sitting on the design side and material testing on the verification side.

**Concrete specifically, and the limits of this evidence**

Retrieval widened from concrete work to circular construction generally, and this matters for what can be claimed: no concrete-work enabler, and no deployed process record or census record of any kind, appears in the material for the circular route. I have no deployed case, and no firm, to name behind circular concrete here, and I will not imply one.

The one concrete-specific item in front of me bears on approval rather than circularity: additive manufacturing (PR3) depends on regulatory and legal concern (RI18), because 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability [5], on standards-grade evidence (DEP83). Regulatory and legal concern (RI18) is activated in 12 of the 50 coded cases. Read this as a warning attached to any novel concrete process, including demountable or reversible systems: the acceptance route has to be planned, and the context establishes these particular acceptance criteria without establishing that they are the only ones that apply.

**What to do with this**

Put the recoverability decision in the connection design and keep concrete components demountable rather than monolithic, since that is the only cited path to material recovery. Build the component data and material passport layer first: it is both the stated precondition for viable circularity and the stated mitigation for the cost uncertainty that otherwise kills the business case. Expect material testing and supply-chain integration to travel with the work. And budget for the certification path if the concrete process itself is novel.
